subsection: 4. Parnell’s fall, Redmond’s leadership and Home Rule’s rivals, 1886–1914

notes.h: The Plan of Campaign and Parnell’s distance from it (1886–1887)
notes.b: Parnell kept a cautious distance from the Plan of Campaign, but his party’s support for tenants kept the land struggle alive.
points: The Plan of Campaign began on estates in 1886, and Parnell did not endorse its collective rent-withholding in public.
Parnell’s concern was to keep Home Rule and the Liberal alliance intact, since the Plan’s evictions and violence alarmed British opinion.
The Plan was a source of conflict within nationalism, and the Papal rescript of 1888 condemned it, which strengthened opponents of the campaign.

notes.h: The Pigott forgeries and the Special Commission (1887–1890)
notes.b: The Times tried to link Parnell to crime, and the forgeries that were its evidence collapsed in 1889.
points: In 1887 The Times published a series of articles under the heading Parnellism and Crime, linking Parnell to the Phoenix Park murders and to agrarian violence.
The main evidence was a set of letters, supposedly signed by Parnell, that approved the Phoenix Park murders; they were forgeries produced by Richard Pigott.
A Special Commission sat from 1888 to 1889 to examine the charges, and Parnell was cleared of approving the murders.
Pigott confessed to forgery in February 1889 and fled abroad, and he took his own life in Madrid in March 1889.
The Pigott affair increased Parnell’s popularity among nationalists, who saw the charges as a conspiracy by the British press and the unionist government.

notes.h: The O’Shea divorce and the split (1890)
notes.b: The O’Shea divorce scandal of 1890 destroyed Parnell’s position with the Liberals and divided his party.
points: Captain William O’Shea, an Irish Party MP, petitioned for divorce in 1890, naming Parnell as co-respondent in the case involving his wife Katharine O’Shea.
Gladstone wrote in November 1890 that Parnell’s continued leadership would damage the Home Rule cause, and the Liberal alliance became conditional on Parnell stepping aside.
The Catholic hierarchy and many Catholic nationalists condemned Parnell’s conduct, and the bishops’ opposition was central to the split.
The Irish Party met in Committee Room 15 at Westminster in December 1890 and voted to keep Parnell as chairman by 44 votes to 29.
The minority who left the party, led by Justin McCarthy, became the anti-Parnellite group, while Parnell’s supporters were called Parnellites.
Parnell fought on in Irish by-elections in 1891, but his health failed, and he died at Brighton on 6 October 1891, aged 45.

notes.b: Gladstone’s second bill passed the Commons but was rejected by the Lords, and the divided party could not force it through.
points: Gladstone introduced a second Home Rule Bill in February 1893, which provided for an Irish legislature with two chambers and for Irish MPs to continue to sit at Westminster in reduced numbers.
The bill passed the Commons in 1893, but the House of Lords rejected it by a large majority in September 1893.
The bill’s defeat showed that the Liberal government could not pass Home Rule without a Lords reform, and it set the agenda for the Parliament Act of 1911.

notes.h: The party in the 1890s and reunion (1900)
notes.b: The divided party lost ground in the 1890s, and reunion under Redmond in 1900 restored the national party machine.
points: The Irish Party was split between Parnellites and anti-Parnellites during the 1890s, and the two groups competed for seats and for the nationalist vote.
The United Irish League, founded in 1898 at Westport, Co. Mayo, by William O’Brien and Davitt, campaigned for the land and against the leadership split.
The reunion of the Irish Party was agreed in 1900, with John Redmond as chairman, and the parties came together under his leadership.
The United Irish League became the party’s grassroots organisation, and it held the party together in the countryside through the land campaign of 1900–1903.

notes.h: Key personality: Charles Stewart Parnell (part 2: 1886–1891 and overall evaluation)
notes.b: The second part of Parnell’s career ended in scandal, but his strategy shaped the party that followed him.
points: As a participant in the Pigott and O’Shea affairs, Parnell faced public charges, and he defended himself in the Commons and in the courts.
Contemporary nationalists remained loyal to him through the split, and the Parnellite group kept his name as a living symbol of resistance.
Contemporary Liberals and the Catholic hierarchy judged his continued leadership a liability for Home Rule after 1890.
Historians judge his achievements as the creation of a disciplined national party and the transformation of the land question, and his failures as the O’Shea scandal and the split.

Parnell’s strengths were his parliamentary skill, his cold discipline and his ability to unite agrarian and parliamentary nationalism; his weaknesses were his dependence on the Liberals and his personal conduct.

notes.b: Redmond led the Irish Party from 1900 to 1918, and his politics centred on Home Rule through constitutional means and alliance with the Liberals.
points: John Redmond (1856–1918) was MP for Waterford from 1891 and the leader of the reunited Irish Party from 1900.
As leader, Redmond held the party together, won the Liberal government’s support for the Third Home Rule Bill, and supported the Parliament Act of 1911.
The Irish Party under Redmond held the balance of power after the 1910 elections, which gave the party decisive influence over the Liberal government.

Redmond was a participant in the constitutional struggle, and he played a central role in the parliamentary passage of the Third Home Rule Bill, which is treated in the notes on the Third Home Rule crisis.
Contemporary nationalists praised him as a constitutional statesman, while the advanced nationalists criticised him for dependence on the Liberals and for the party’s lack of militancy.

Historians differ over Redmond: some see him as a realistic constitutionalist who achieved Home Rule on the statute book, while others see him as too dependent on British goodwill to defend Irish national interests.
Redmond’s Home Rule Act was suspended for the duration of the First World War when war broke out, and Redmond’s support for British recruitment divided nationalists.

notes.b: Arthur Griffith’s Sinn Féin proposed an alternative to Home Rule through abstention and economic self-sufficiency rather than a Westminster parliament.
points: Arthur Griffith founded the weekly The United Irishman in 1899 and used it to promote a policy of Irish self-reliance.
Griffith founded Cumann na nGaedheal in 1900, a small group that promoted Irish industry and self-government.
In The Resurrection of Hungary, published in 1904, Griffith argued that Ireland should follow the Hungarian model of dual monarchy, a separate parliament under a shared crown.
Sinn Féin, as a party, was founded in 1905 by a national council, and its programme included abstention from Westminster and economic protectionism.
The party’s support was small: it fielded few candidates, and its candidate in the North Leitrim by-election of 1908 did not win the seat.
After 1908 the party declined, and its ideas were absorbed by later separatist groups, including the Irish Volunteers.

notes.h: The IRB revival and the Irish Volunteers (1907–1914)
notes.b: Separatist groups revived after 1907, and the Irish Volunteers were founded in 1913 as a response to the Ulster Volunteers.
points: Tom Clarke returned from the United States in 1907 and became a leading figure in the revived Irish Republican Brotherhood, alongside Bulmer Hobson and Seán Mac Diarmada.
Eoin MacNeill’s article The North Began, published in 1913, argued that the Ulster Volunteers had set an example that nationalists should follow.
The Irish Volunteers were founded at a meeting in the Rotunda, Dublin, in November 1913, with MacNeill as chief of staff.
Cumann na mBan, the women’s auxiliary, was founded in April 1914 to support the Volunteers.
The Howth gun-running of 26 July 1914 landed rifles at Howth, Co. Dublin, from the yacht Asgard, and was followed by a second landing at Kilcoole, Co. Wicklow.
Redmond secured a share of the Volunteer committee’s control in 1914, and his supporters joined the Volunteers in large numbers.

The Volunteers split in September 1914, after Redmond’s speech at Woodenbridge, Co. Wicklow, in which he called on Volunteers to fight in the war; the majority followed him into the National Volunteers, and a minority kept the Irish Volunteers under MacNeill.

notes.h: Assessment: Parnell’s legacy and Redmond’s leadership
notes.b: Judgements on the period contrast constitutional success with the rise of separatist and militant alternatives.
points: Redmond’s achievement was to bring Home Rule to the statute book by 1914, through the Parliament Act of 1911 and the Home Rule Act.
Redmond’s limit was that the Home Rule Act was suspended until after the war, and the Irish Volunteers split over support for Britain.
Contemporary Unionists judged Home Rule a betrayal, while nationalists judged Redmond’s achievement a victory won against British and Ulster opposition.
Separatists such as Griffith and the IRB judged the constitutional strategy a failure, which led them to seek a different route to independence.

keyTerms.definition: The demand for an Irish parliament to manage domestic affairs, which Redmond’s party pursued through constitutional means until 1914.
The aim of independence from the United Kingdom, as opposed to self-government within it, which Sinn Féin and the IRB pursued.
The development of armed volunteer forces, such as the Irish Volunteers, as a political instrument to achieve a national aim.
Griffith’s party, founded in 1905, which promoted abstention from Westminster, dual monarchy and economic self-sufficiency.
The armed nationalist force founded in November 1913 in Dublin to match the Ulster Volunteers, which split in September 1914.
The secret separatist organisation, known as the IRB, which was revived after 1907 under Tom Clarke and Bulmer Hobson.
The women’s association founded in April 1914 to support the Irish Volunteers.
The Hungarian model, under which Hungary had its own parliament while sharing a crown with Austria, which Griffith proposed for Ireland.
